title: Artificial Intelligence Foundations
intro: Human and machine intelligence, the Turing Test, AI history, categories and core domains.

sec.s: Artificial intelligence (AI) is one of the most influential areas of modern computing.

b.x: Artificial intelligence (AI) is one of the most influential areas of modern computing. It concerns the design of computer systems that can perform tasks associated with abilities such as learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, language use, planning, and decision-making. AI is not a single program or device. It is a broad field that includes many methods, from systems built with explicit rules to machine-learning models that identify patterns in data and deep-learning networks that learn complex representations.

AI is now used in search engines, translation tools, recommendation systems, medical image analysis, fraud detection, voice assistants, industrial robots, navigation systems, and generative tools that produce text, images, audio, and code. However, the existence of these applications does not mean that every AI system thinks like a human. A system may perform one task exceptionally well while having little ability to perform unrelated tasks. A chess program can defeat world-class players without being able to cook a meal, understand a social situation, or learn a new physical skill in the way a person does.

To understand AI clearly, it is useful to study several connected questions. What distinguishes human intelligence from machine intelligence? How should artificial intelligence be defined? Why did Alan Turing propose a conversational test for machine intelligence? How did AI develop historically, and why did it experience periods known as AI winters? What do the terms narrow AI, general AI, and super AI mean? Finally, how do data science, computer vision, and natural language processing contribute to modern AI?

These questions are related but not identical. A definition describes the field; a test evaluates a particular kind of behaviour; a historical account explains how research developed; categories describe different scopes of capability; and core domains identify important problem areas and methods. Keeping these distinctions clear prevents common misunderstandings.

sec.s: Human intelligence is a broad collection of cognitive abilities that allows people to learn from…

b.x: 2.1 Meaning of human intelligence

Human intelligence is a broad collection of cognitive abilities that allows people to learn from experience, understand situations, reason about problems, communicate, plan, adapt, and act in changing environments. It is not a single simple skill. Human beings combine language, memory, perception, attention, social understanding, physical experience, emotional responses, creativity, and practical judgement.

A person can use knowledge acquired in one situation to help solve a different problem. Someone who learns the basic idea of fractions may later apply it while cooking, dividing a bill, or measuring materials. This transfer of learning is important: people often use concepts flexibly in circumstances they have not encountered before. Humans can also learn from relatively few examples, ask other people for clarification, use context to interpret incomplete information, and recognize when they do not know something.

Human intelligence develops through a combination of biological factors, experience, education, culture, social interaction, and the environment. People learn not only from formal instruction but also from observation, experimentation, mistakes, play, and physical interaction with the world. Their learning is embodied: perception and action are closely connected. For example, understanding how to ride a bicycle requires more than memorizing a written description. It involves balance, movement, feedback, and repeated practice.

Human intelligence also has important limitations. People forget information, make reasoning errors, become distracted, rely on stereotypes, misjudge probabilities, and allow emotion or social pressure to influence decisions. Human memory is not a perfect recording of events. Two people can interpret the same event differently. Intelligence therefore does not guarantee accuracy, fairness, wisdom, or good judgement.
2.2 Meaning of machine intelligence

Machine intelligence refers to the ability of a computer-based system to carry out tasks that are commonly associated with intelligent behaviour. Such tasks can include classifying information, detecting patterns, predicting outcomes, optimizing a process, understanding or generating language, recognizing objects, planning actions, and solving formal problems.

Machines do not all achieve these abilities in the same way. A traditional rule-based system follows rules written by programmers. A search algorithm explores possible solutions according to a defined procedure. A machine-learning system uses examples or experience represented as data to adjust a model. A deep-learning system uses layers of mathematical operations to learn complex patterns from large datasets. A hybrid system may combine rules, learned models, databases, search, and external tools.

For example, a spam filter may learn from messages labelled as spam or legitimate. During training, its parameters are adjusted so that the model becomes better at distinguishing the categories. When a new message arrives, the model estimates whether it resembles spam. It does not need to understand the message in the same broad human sense as a person; it needs to identify useful statistical patterns for the task.

Machine intelligence is often measured through a clearly defined objective: accuracy, response time, reward, cost, or another performance measure. This can make machines extremely effective at tasks where the input, output, and evaluation criteria are well specified. Yet a high score on one benchmark does not prove that a system has general intelligence or human-like understanding.
2.3 Important similarities

Human and machine intelligence can both support problem-solving, pattern recognition, prediction, planning, and language-related tasks. Both can use information from previous examples to improve performance in some settings. Both may produce answers that are incorrect. Both can benefit from feedback and from a carefully designed learning environment.

A machine-learning model can, for example, examine thousands of labelled photographs and learn patterns that help it identify cats. A child may learn to recognize cats after seeing a smaller number of examples, although the child’s learning is supported by extensive prior knowledge about objects, animals, motion, and the world. In both cases, experience contributes to recognition, but the underlying learning processes are different.

Both people and machines can also appear to perform a task by using internal representations. Humans form concepts and mental models, while AI systems may learn numerical representations, decision rules, or symbolic structures. The similarity in outward performance does not establish that the internal processes are the same.
2.4 Major differences

A. Biological versus computational foundations Human intelligence emerges from the brain and body, which are biological systems shaped by evolution and development. Machine intelligence runs on hardware and software designed and built by people. Artificial neural networks take some inspiration from networks of biological neurons, but they are mathematical systems and should not be treated as literal copies of the human brain.

B. General flexibility versus specialization Humans can usually move between many everyday activities, although expertise varies. Most deployed AI systems are designed, trained, or evaluated for a narrower range of tasks. A language model may answer questions, summarize documents, and write code, but it can still make mistakes in arithmetic, factual recall, physical reasoning, or unfamiliar situations. Broad performance across several tasks is not the same as reliable human-level general intelligence.

C. Learning requirements People often learn from a small number of examples and can use background knowledge to interpret them. Many modern AI systems require large datasets, substantial computing resources, carefully prepared training processes, and extensive evaluation. Some machine-learning methods can learn from relatively little data, and research continues to improve data efficiency, but the comparison depends on the task and the learning setup.

D. Experience and embodiment Humans learn through sight, sound, touch, movement, emotion, and interaction with physical and social environments. A text-only model is trained primarily on text and does not automatically possess the experiences described in that text. A vision model can process images but does not necessarily understand the practical meaning of an object in the way a person who manipulates it might. Robots can interact physically, but reliable real-world interaction remains challenging.

E. Goals and motivation People have biological needs, personal goals, emotions, and social relationships. An AI system operates according to objectives, instructions, reward signals, or other mechanisms specified through its design and use. A system can be optimized to achieve a goal without having human desires or subjective motivation. Describing a model as “wanting” something can be a convenient metaphor, but it should not be confused with evidence of human-like experience.

F. Understanding and meaning Humans connect language to perception, lived experience, social context, and a large store of world knowledge. AI systems can learn powerful statistical relationships and produce contextually appropriate outputs, but whether and in what sense a particular system understands meaning is debated. Fluent language alone cannot settle the philosophical question of understanding.

G. Consistency and scale Computers can process large volumes of data quickly and repeat a defined operation consistently. Human performance can vary with fatigue, attention, and context. Nevertheless, machine systems can also behave inconsistently, fail under distribution shifts, inherit errors from data, or produce confident but false outputs. Consistency is conditional on the system and task.

H. Energy and computation The brain is highly energy-efficient relative to many large-scale computing workloads, although comparisons are difficult because brains and computers perform different kinds of work. Training large AI models can require significant computing infrastructure and electricity. Inference costs vary widely according to model size, hardware, and usage.
2.5 A practical comparison

Consider the task of identifying a dangerous situation on a road. A human driver combines visual information with context, memory, physical intuition, social expectations, and an understanding of possible consequences. A computer-vision system can detect vehicles, lanes, pedestrians, and traffic signs, sometimes at high speed and with excellent performance under its tested conditions. However, it may fail when lighting changes, road markings are unusual, an object is partly hidden, or an uncommon event occurs. A reliable driving system therefore needs more than one image classifier: it requires perception, prediction, planning, control, testing, and safeguards.

The comparison illustrates a general principle: the best way to evaluate AI is not to ask whether machines are simply “as intelligent as humans.” Instead, ask which task is being performed, under what conditions, using what evidence, with what error rate, and with what consequences if the system fails.
2.6 Is machine intelligence necessarily inferior?

No. Machines can exceed human performance in particular areas. They can search large databases, perform repeated calculations, examine many images, or evaluate millions of possible game positions faster than a person. A specialised model can detect subtle statistical patterns that are difficult for a human to notice.

At the same time, excellence in a narrow task does not imply superiority in every cognitive activity. Human and machine strengths are different. A useful approach is often to combine them: machines can process information and propose options, while people provide context, ethical judgement, responsibility, and oversight. This arrangement is sometimes called human-AI collaboration or human-in-the-loop decision-making.
2.7 Intelligence, consciousness, and sentience

Intelligence, consciousness, and sentience are related concepts but should not be treated as synonyms. Intelligence usually refers to abilities such as learning, reasoning, adaptation, and problem-solving. Consciousness may refer to subjective experience or awareness. Sentience commonly refers to the capacity to have experiences, particularly experiences with a positive or negative quality.

A system may display intelligent behaviour without there being evidence that it has subjective experience. Conversely, the question of whether a machine could ever be conscious is a philosophical and scientific issue that does not have a universally accepted answer. Current performance in language or image tasks is not, by itself, proof of consciousness. This distinction is important when interpreting claims about advanced AI.

sec.s: Artificial intelligence is a field of computer science concerned with creating and studying computational…

b.x: 3.1 A general definition

Artificial intelligence is a field of computer science concerned with creating and studying computational systems that can perform tasks associated with abilities such as learning, reasoning, perception, language processing, planning, and decision-making.

There is no single definition accepted in every context. Some definitions focus on systems that act intelligently; others emphasize rational agents, learning, or the automation of tasks that normally require human intelligence. The variation exists because intelligence itself is complex and because AI includes very different methods and applications.

A practical definition is: AI is the design of computational agents that use data, representations, rules, learning algorithms, or other computational methods to perceive relevant information, infer or select actions, and pursue specified objectives in an environment.

This definition includes both traditional systems and modern learning-based models. A rule-based medical expert system, a chess program, an image classifier, and a language model can all fall within AI, even though their designs and capabilities differ.
3.2 The rational-agent perspective

In AI, an agent is an entity that receives information from its environment and takes actions. A software agent may receive data through files, sensors, an API, or a user interface. A robot may receive information from cameras and other sensors and act through motors. An intelligent agent selects actions in relation to a goal or performance measure.

The rational-agent perspective asks what action is appropriate given the available information, the agent’s knowledge, and its objective. Rationality does not mean that the system is omniscient or always correct. It means that the action is selected in a way that is appropriate to the information and objective available to the agent.

For example, a route-planning system receives a starting point, destination, road information, and perhaps traffic conditions. It evaluates possible routes and recommends one according to factors such as estimated travel time, distance, tolls, or user preferences. The system does not need to think exactly like a human driver to perform this useful task.
3.3 Major approaches within AI

A. Rule-based or symbolic AI Symbolic AI represents knowledge using symbols, logical expressions, facts, and explicit rules. For example, a simple rule might state: IF the temperature is above a specified threshold AND a sensor indicates smoke, THEN raise an alarm. Symbolic methods can be interpretable and useful when rules are known, but they may be difficult to maintain when the environment is complex or uncertain.

B. Search and planning Search algorithms explore possible states or action sequences to find a solution. A chess program may examine possible moves and evaluate resulting board positions. A planning system may search for a sequence of actions that achieves a goal while respecting constraints. The quality of the result depends on the representation, search strategy, evaluation function, and available resources.

C. Machine learning Machine learning is a subfield of AI in which systems learn patterns from data or experience instead of relying entirely on manually written rules. In supervised learning, examples include input data and target labels. In unsupervised learning, the system looks for structure without the same kind of explicit target labels. In reinforcement learning, an agent learns through interaction and feedback often represented as rewards.

D. Deep learning Deep learning uses neural networks with multiple layers to learn representations and patterns. It has contributed substantially to image recognition, speech processing, language modelling, and generative AI. Deep learning often performs well with large datasets and substantial computation, but it can be difficult to interpret and may require careful evaluation and safeguards.

E. Probabilistic reasoning AI systems often need to reason under uncertainty. Probabilistic methods represent uncertainty and estimate how likely different outcomes are given available evidence. A medical decision-support system, for instance, may estimate the probability of a condition based on symptoms and test results. Such estimates support decisions but do not automatically replace professional judgement.

F. Robotics and embodied AI Robotics combines perception, planning, control, and physical action. A robot may need to locate objects, avoid obstacles, grasp items, and adjust to unexpected movement. Real-world environments contain noise, friction, changing lighting, and incomplete information, making physical intelligence particularly challenging.
3.4 AI, machine learning, and deep learning

These terms are often confused. AI is the broadest field. Machine learning is a set of methods within AI that learn from data or experience. Deep learning is a family of machine-learning methods based on multilayer neural networks.
A simple hierarchy is
Artificial Intelligence Machine Learning Deep Learning

The hierarchy is useful but not exhaustive: AI also includes approaches that do not depend on machine learning, such as classical search and some rule-based systems. Machine learning can be used without deep learning, for example with decision trees, linear models, or support-vector machines.

Suppose a developer creates a program that identifies whether a number is even by checking whether its remainder after division by two is zero. This is conventional programming, not normally considered AI. A program that searches for the best move in a complex game may be AI even if it uses explicit search and evaluation rules. A model trained on thousands of examples to classify images is machine learning, and if it uses a deep neural network, it is deep learning.
3.5 Why definitions matter

Definitions influence research goals, public expectations, regulation, and evaluation. If every automated system is called AI, the term becomes too broad to be informative. If AI is defined only as human-like thought, many useful systems may be excluded. A careful definition identifies the capability, method, and context under discussion.

It is also important to separate capability from reliability. A system may be capable of generating an answer but not reliably generate a correct answer. A system may produce human-like language without possessing human-like understanding. AI evaluation should therefore include measurable performance, robustness, safety, fairness, and the consequences of errors.

sec.t: The Turing Test: Meaning, Method, Importance, and Limitations
sec.s: In 1950, British mathematician and computer scientist Alan Turing published “Computing Machinery and…

b.x: 4.1 Historical background

In 1950, British mathematician and computer scientist Alan Turing published “Computing Machinery and Intelligence.” Instead of treating the broad question “Can machines think?” as a straightforward yes-or-no question, Turing proposed a practical thought experiment known as the imitation game. The idea became widely known as the Turing Test.

Turing was responding to a difficult problem: the word “think” is ambiguous, and people may disagree about what evidence would prove that a machine thinks. A behavioural test offered a more concrete way to investigate whether a computer could display conversational behaviour that people might mistake for a human’s.

The test is historically important because it shifted discussion from abstract declarations toward observable performance. It also encouraged researchers to consider language, reasoning, knowledge, and conversation as parts of intelligent behaviour.
4.2 Basic setup

In the familiar text-based version, a human evaluator communicates with two unseen participants: one human and one machine. The evaluator asks questions and reads their answers without knowing which participant is the computer. If the evaluator cannot reliably distinguish the machine from the human through the conversation, the machine may be judged to have succeeded under the test’s conditions.

The test is not simply a quiz containing factual questions. An evaluator might ask about everyday situations, jokes, preferences, reasoning, ambiguous language, or a recent conversation. The machine needs to respond in a way that sustains the interaction. The exact outcome depends on the questions, duration, participants, and criteria used.
4.3 What the test attempts to measure

The Turing Test focuses on human-like conversational behaviour. It asks whether a machine can produce responses that are difficult for a human evaluator to distinguish from human responses in a particular interaction.

This is a behavioural criterion, not a direct measurement of a machine’s internal mental state. Passing would show that the system can imitate or produce convincing conversational behaviour under the specified conditions. It would not, by itself, establish consciousness, emotions, genuine intentions, or a complete human-like understanding of the world.
4.4 Why the test was significant
First, it made the question of machine intelligence more operational. Rather than arguing endlessly about the definition of thought, researchers could examine performance in a structured interaction.

Second, it highlighted the importance of language. Human conversation requires more than producing isolated words: it involves context, reference, turn-taking, explanation, and adapting responses to what another person says.
Third, it influenced public discussion about intelligent machines. The test became a familiar way to ask whether a computer can appear human in conversation.

Fourth, it stimulated debate about what counts as evidence of intelligence. Some researchers emphasize observable behaviour and practical capability, while others argue that internal processes, grounding, learning, or understanding must also be considered.
4.5 Limitations and criticisms

A. Imitation is not identical to intelligence A system might deceive an evaluator by giving vague answers, changing the subject, pretending to have limited knowledge, or exploiting the evaluator’s assumptions. Such strategies could improve the chance of appearing human without demonstrating broad reasoning ability.

B. Human-like behaviour is not the only form of intelligence An AI system may solve difficult mathematical problems, optimize a power grid, or detect a disease pattern without communicating like a human. A conversational test may fail to recognize these forms of useful intelligence.

C. Results depend on test design The evaluator’s expertise, the length of the conversation, the topics asked about, and the scoring rules can affect the outcome. A short conversation may not reveal weaknesses that become apparent during a longer technical or practical task.

D. Fluency can create false confidence Modern language models can produce fluent and persuasive responses. Yet they may state false facts, misunderstand constraints, invent sources, or fail on tasks that require reliable multi-step reasoning. Natural language quality is therefore not a complete measure of competence.

E. It does not test all dimensions of intelligence The test does not directly assess physical interaction, long-term learning, autonomous planning, scientific discovery, emotional experience, moral judgement, or dependable performance in high-stakes environments.

F. It does not settle consciousness Even if a machine produces conversation indistinguishable from a human’s, the result does not prove that the machine has subjective experience. Behaviour and consciousness are distinct questions.
4.6 The Turing Test in the age of conversational AI

Contemporary chatbots have made the test newly relevant, but also more complicated. A system can generate grammatically correct, contextually appropriate text over many topics. It may explain a concept, write a poem, summarize a document, or imitate a conversational style. These abilities are impressive, yet they can coexist with errors, inconsistent reasoning, limited grounding, and sensitivity to how a prompt is phrased.

A responsible evaluation of modern AI should use several forms of testing. These may include task-specific benchmarks, adversarial tests, human evaluation, factual verification, robustness checks, privacy and security assessments, and real-world monitoring. A single conversation is not enough to establish that a model is safe or generally intelligent.
4.7 A simple illustrative example

Imagine an evaluator asks two hidden participants: “Why might someone carry an umbrella on a cloudy day?” A human might say, “They expect rain, or they prefer to be prepared.” A chatbot may give a similar answer. This exchange alone reveals little about the system’s broader capabilities.

The evaluator might then ask a question involving a long sequence of constraints, a subtle reference to earlier text, or a situation requiring uncertainty. The system’s performance may vary. The lesson is that conversational similarity is one useful observation, not a universal certificate of intelligence.
4.8 Overall significance

The Turing Test remains a landmark in the philosophy and history of AI. Its greatest contribution is not that it provides a final definition of intelligence, but that it established a memorable behavioural framework for examining machine performance. It should be treated as one perspective among many rather than a complete scientific test for all forms of intelligence.

sec.s: The history of AI reaches back beyond the first electronic computers.

b.x: 5.1 Intellectual foundations before modern computers

The history of AI reaches back beyond the first electronic computers. Philosophers studied logic, reasoning, knowledge, and the nature of the mind. Mathematicians developed formal systems that could represent statements and derive conclusions. These ideas helped create the possibility that aspects of reasoning might be expressed in mechanical procedures.

In the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, developments in mathematical logic and computation clarified what formal systems and algorithms could do. George Boole developed an algebraic approach to logic. Later work by logicians and mathematicians explored formal reasoning and computability. These developments did not themselves create modern AI, but they supplied important conceptual foundations.

The rise of electronic computing in the 1940s provided machines capable of carrying out complex sequences of operations. Researchers began to consider whether computers could do more than arithmetic. Could they play games, prove theorems, learn patterns, translate language, or model aspects of human problem-solving?
5.2 Alan Turing and the foundations of computational intelligence

Alan Turing was a central figure in the theory of computation. His work helped clarify the idea of a general-purpose computing machine and the limits of mechanical computation. In 1950, he directly addressed machine intelligence in “Computing Machinery and Intelligence,” introducing the imitation game.

Turing’s work did not solve AI, but it helped frame questions that researchers continue to discuss: What behaviour would count as intelligent? Can reasoning be represented computationally? How should we evaluate machine performance? What limitations arise from the nature of computation?
5.3 Early AI programs

During the 1950s, researchers developed programs that could solve formal problems. The Logic Theorist, created by Allen Newell, Herbert A. Simon, and Cliff Shaw, demonstrated that a computer could prove selected mathematical theorems. It used symbolic representations and search strategies rather than learning from a large modern dataset.

Another early program, the General Problem Solver, aimed to model problem-solving through a general framework. Although its practical reach was limited, it expressed an ambitious idea: some reasoning processes might be represented as reusable methods rather than separate instructions for every problem.

Early programs often operated in simplified environments. A program that solved a puzzle could rely on precise rules and a small set of possible states. Real-world tasks were more difficult because language is ambiguous, the world is uncertain, and the number of possible situations can be enormous.
5.4 The rise of optimism

Early demonstrations encouraged the belief that rapid progress might lead to broadly intelligent machines. Researchers found that computers could play games, solve logical puzzles, and manipulate symbolic expressions. Funding increased, and AI laboratories developed at universities and research institutions.

However, success in small demonstrations did not translate automatically into robust performance in the real world. Many systems depended on carefully controlled conditions, simplified problems, and knowledge explicitly supplied by developers. The gap between a convincing prototype and a reliable general system became a recurring theme in AI history.

sec.s: The Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, held in 1956 at Dartmouth College in…

b.x: 6.1 Background and proposal

The Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, held in 1956 at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire, is widely regarded as a foundational event in the establishment of AI as a research field. The proposal was associated with John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon. John McCarthy is credited with introducing the term “artificial intelligence” in this context.

The proposal argued that aspects of learning and intelligence might be described precisely enough for machines to simulate them. It suggested research into language use, abstraction, concept formation, problem-solving, and machine improvement. The idea was ambitious: instead of treating computers solely as calculators, researchers would explore whether they could perform activities associated with intelligent minds.
6.2 Why the conference mattered

The conference helped establish AI as a recognizable research agenda. It brought researchers together around common questions and helped shape a vocabulary for discussing machine intelligence. It did not produce a complete intelligent machine, nor did it resolve the central scientific challenges. Its importance lies in launching and organizing a sustained research programme.
Several influential themes emerged from the early AI community

x: Symbolic representation of knowledge.
Logical reasoning and theorem proving.
Problem-solving through search.
Language processing.
Learning and adaptation.
The possibility of machines performing tasks previously associated with human cognition.

b.x: These themes later developed into distinct areas of research. Some remain central today, while others have been combined with statistical learning, neural networks, robotics, and large-scale data processing.
6.3 Key participants

John McCarthy helped establish AI as a named field and later contributed to programming languages and formal reasoning. Marvin Minsky became a major figure in AI research and helped develop influential ideas about representation and cognition. Nathaniel Rochester contributed expertise in computing and engineering. Claude Shannon, known for foundational work in information theory, helped connect information, computation, and intelligent behaviour.

The participants did not all agree on how intelligence should be reproduced or which methods would succeed. AI developed through competition and collaboration among different schools of thought, including symbolic approaches, connectionist approaches, probabilistic methods, and later data-driven deep learning.
6.4 What the conference did not achieve

It is important not to exaggerate the conference’s immediate results. The meeting did not create modern AI systems in a single summer. The available computers had limited memory and processing power, datasets were small by modern standards, and many scientific problems were not yet understood. The conference established a field and an ambitious agenda, while the subsequent decades involved repeated progress, setbacks, and changes in methodology.
6.5 Lasting influence

The Dartmouth event is remembered because it marked a transition from scattered investigations of machine reasoning to a more clearly identified field. It also illustrates a recurring pattern in science: a powerful research vision can organize work long before the vision is fully achievable. Modern AI continues to investigate many of the original questions, although its methods and scale have changed dramatically.

sec.t: AI Winters and Periods of Renewed Progress
sec.s: An AI winter is a period in which enthusiasm, funding, and expectations for AI decline, often because the…

b.x: 7.1 Meaning of an AI winter

An AI winter is a period in which enthusiasm, funding, and expectations for AI decline, often because the technology fails to deliver promised results. The term does not mean that all research stops or that every AI technique becomes useless. Instead, attention and investment may fall after a period of exaggerated expectations or disappointing practical outcomes.

Histories often identify two major periods of reduced enthusiasm: one beginning in the 1970s and another around the late 1980s and early 1990s. The exact dates differ by country, funding programme, and subfield. Some researchers continued to make important contributions during these periods, even while public and institutional confidence declined.
7.2 Why AI winters occurred

A. Excessive expectations Early predictions sometimes assumed that human-level intelligence was only a few years away. In reality, intelligence involves language, perception, common-sense knowledge, learning, uncertainty, and adaptation. These capabilities proved much harder to combine than early demonstrations suggested.

B. Limited computing power Early computers had far less memory and processing capacity than modern systems. Many algorithms that looked promising on small examples became too slow or expensive when applied to realistic problems.

C. The combinatorial explosion A system may face an enormous number of possible actions or interpretations. The number of possibilities can grow rapidly as a problem becomes larger. Search methods that work on small puzzles may become impractical in complex environments unless strong heuristics, approximations, or constraints are available.

D. The common-sense problem Humans rely on extensive background knowledge that is rarely stated explicitly. A person knows that a glass may break when dropped, that water can spill, and that a person cannot normally be in two distant places at once. Encoding this broad knowledge in formal rules proved difficult. Systems often failed when a situation required information that had not been explicitly represented.

E. Narrow performance An AI program could succeed in a demonstration while failing in new circumstances. Researchers found that systems often relied on the specific structure of the examples or assumptions built into the task. Practical users require reliability under variation, not just success in a controlled demonstration.

F. Funding and evaluation pressures When projects promised dramatic results but delivered limited practical value, sponsors became more cautious. Government agencies and commercial organizations had finite resources and expected measurable outcomes. Funding reductions then made it harder for some research programmes to continue.
7.3 The first AI winter

The first major AI winter is commonly associated with the 1970s. Early optimism was challenged by critical evaluations of machine translation, neural-network limitations, and the difficulty of scaling symbolic systems. In the United Kingdom, the 1973 Lighthill report criticized the progress and prospects of AI research in several areas, contributing to reduced support for some British research programmes. In the United States, funding priorities also shifted, and some projects faced tighter evaluation.

This period did not erase AI research. Work continued in logic, planning, robotics, language processing, and neural-network theory. The lesson was that impressive demonstrations and bold forecasts needed to be matched by evidence of generality, scalability, and practical value.
7.4 Expert systems and renewed interest

During the late 1970s and 1980s, expert systems revived commercial interest. These systems represented specialist knowledge as rules and used inference mechanisms to draw conclusions. They were applied in areas such as equipment configuration, diagnosis, and technical support.

An expert system might contain rules supplied by domain specialists. For example, if certain symptoms and test results were present, the system might recommend that a clinician consider a particular diagnosis. The system’s performance depended heavily on the quality, completeness, and maintenance of its knowledge base.

Expert systems were valuable in constrained domains, but they had limitations. Rules were expensive to collect and update, exceptions multiplied, and systems could become brittle when faced with unfamiliar cases. Their maintenance costs and limited flexibility contributed to declining enthusiasm for some commercial products.
7.5 The second AI winter

The late 1980s and early 1990s saw another decline in parts of the AI industry. Some specialized AI hardware markets weakened, and many expert-system products proved costly to maintain or less adaptable than buyers expected. Commercial promises had often exceeded the systems’ practical capabilities.

Again, the winter was not a complete halt in scientific progress. Researchers continued developing statistical learning, probabilistic reasoning, computer vision, speech recognition, robotics, and neural networks. Some methods that later became important were refined during periods when AI attracted less public attention.
7.6 Why the AI field recovered
AI progress depends on several interacting factors

x: Better computing hardware.
Larger and more accessible datasets.
Improved algorithms and mathematical techniques.
More effective evaluation methods.
Practical applications with measurable value.
Stronger software and data infrastructure.
Research across statistics, neuroscience, linguistics, mathematics, and engineering.

b.x: Machine learning increasingly offered an alternative to manually encoding every rule. Instead of specifying every feature and decision, developers could train models on examples. Statistical methods became more practical as computing resources and data availability improved.
7.7 Lessons from AI winters
First, scientific progress is rarely a straight line. Breakthroughs can be followed by periods of correction, consolidation, and more realistic expectations.
Second, a demonstration is not the same as a dependable product. Systems must work under real conditions, handle edge cases, and justify their cost.
Third, predictions about general intelligence should be treated cautiously. A rapid improvement in one benchmark does not guarantee a similar improvement across all tasks.
Fourth, funding and public attention can fluctuate. Researchers and organizations benefit from setting clear objectives, measuring performance, and acknowledging limitations.
Finally, AI winters demonstrate that disappointing periods can still produce valuable knowledge. Failed approaches reveal the complexity of the problem and help the field refine its questions.

sec.t: Major Historical Milestones Leading to Modern AI

b.x: The following timeline is selective. AI history includes many parallel developments, and no single list can capture every contribution.

1830s–1840s: Charles Babbage designed concepts for mechanical general-purpose computation, while Ada Lovelace discussed how such a machine might manipulate symbols according to rules. These ideas preceded electronic computing and are often included in the broader history of computational thought.
1854: George Boole published work that helped establish algebraic logic, contributing to the mathematical representation of logical operations.
1936: Alan Turing described an abstract computing machine that became foundational to the theory of computation. The work helped formalize the idea of algorithms and general-purpose computation.
1940s: Electronic digital computers were developed and used for scientific and military tasks. Their emergence made it possible to test ideas about computation on practical machines.
1943: Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts published a mathematical model of simplified neural activity. Their work influenced later thinking about artificial neural networks.

1949: Donald Hebb proposed a theory of learning through changes in connections between neurons. The broad idea that connection strengths can change with experience later influenced neural-network research.
1950: Alan Turing published “Computing Machinery and Intelligence” and proposed the imitation game, now associated with the Turing Test.
1951: Early machine-learning and game-playing experiments explored how computers could improve or choose moves in constrained tasks.
1955–1956: The Logic Theorist was developed by Allen Newell, Herbert A. Simon, and Cliff Shaw. It demonstrated that a computer could prove selected mathematical theorems using symbolic reasoning.
1956: The Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence helped establish AI as a distinct research field and popularized the name “artificial intelligence.”

Late 1950s: Frank Rosenblatt developed the perceptron, an early learning model inspired by simplified ideas about neurons. Perceptrons could learn certain classifications but had important limitations.
1958: John McCarthy developed Lisp, a programming language that became influential in symbolic AI research.

1960s: Researchers created programs for games, symbolic reasoning, language experiments, and robotics. Systems such as ELIZA, developed by Joseph Weizenbaum in the 1960s, simulated aspects of conversation using pattern-based responses. ELIZA showed how people could perceive understanding in a system that used relatively simple mechanisms.

1966: The ALPAC report in the United States questioned the progress and practical value of machine translation at the time. It contributed to reduced support for some translation research, illustrating the risks of unrealistic expectations.

Late 1960s–early 1970s: Researchers developed mobile robots and early systems that combined perception, planning, and action in restricted environments. These systems exposed the difficulty of integrating separate capabilities.

1970s: Research encountered limitations involving computational resources, common-sense knowledge, and the generalization of early systems. Reduced funding in some regions contributed to the first AI winter.

1972: Prolog, a logic programming language, was developed by Alain Colmerauer and colleagues. It became important in symbolic reasoning and later in some language and knowledge-processing applications.
1970s–1980s: Expert systems represented specialist knowledge using rules and inference engines. They achieved useful results in some constrained commercial and technical settings.

1980s: Research into neural networks advanced, including renewed interest in backpropagation as a practical method for training multilayer networks. The algorithm allowed errors to be propagated backward through a network to update parameters.
Late 1980s–early 1990s: Commercial difficulties in expert systems and specialized AI hardware contributed to another AI winter in parts of the industry.

1990s: Statistical machine learning became increasingly influential. Researchers developed and applied methods such as support-vector machines, Bayesian networks, decision trees, and improved speech-recognition techniques.

1997: IBM’s Deep Blue defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a match. This was a landmark in specialized game-playing systems, but it did not demonstrate general intelligence: the system was designed for chess.

2000s: The growth of the internet, digital storage, sensors, and computing infrastructure made large datasets increasingly available. Machine learning became useful in search, advertising, recommendations, speech, and other applications.

2006: Geoffrey Hinton and collaborators helped renew interest in deep neural networks through work on learning multilayer representations. This period contributed to the broader revival of deep learning.

2009: The ImageNet project helped provide a large labelled image dataset that became influential in computer-vision research. Large datasets made it possible to train and compare models at a scale that had previously been difficult.

2011: IBM Watson defeated human champions on the quiz show Jeopardy! The achievement demonstrated strong performance in a structured question-answering competition, though it relied on a specialized system and did not imply human-like general intelligence.

2012: AlexNet, a deep convolutional neural network, achieved a major result in the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge. Its performance helped establish deep learning as a leading approach in computer vision. GPU computing, large datasets, and neural-network techniques all contributed.

2014: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) were introduced by Ian Goodfellow and colleagues. GANs trained competing neural networks to generate samples resembling training data and became influential in image generation and related research.

2016: DeepMind’s AlphaGo defeated Go champion Lee Sedol. Go had long been considered difficult for computer programs because of its enormous search space and reliance on strategic judgement. AlphaGo combined deep neural networks with search and reinforcement-learning techniques.

2017: The paper “Attention Is All You Need” introduced the Transformer architecture. Attention mechanisms allow models to weigh relationships among elements in a sequence. Transformers later became central to many large language models and multimodal systems.

2018: Transformer-based language models and pretraining methods advanced rapidly. Large-scale pretraining followed by task-specific adaptation became a major approach to language understanding and generation.

2020: Large language models demonstrated increasingly capable few-shot and in-context learning behaviours. Research also expanded in protein-structure prediction, image generation, reinforcement learning, and scientific applications.
2021: AlphaFold2 demonstrated highly influential performance in predicting many protein structures, illustrating how AI could contribute to biological research. Text-to-image research also advanced.

2022: ChatGPT brought conversational generative AI to a broad public audience. Text-to-image systems became widely visible, increasing public awareness of generative models and their potential uses and risks.

2023: Generative AI tools became increasingly integrated into software, education, customer support, research, and creative workflows. Models expanded in tool use and multimodal processing, while concerns about reliability, privacy, bias, copyright, and misuse received greater attention.

2024–2026: AI development continued toward more capable multimodal models, longer-context processing, tool-using systems, coding assistance, reasoning-focused methods, and deployment in products and workflows. Capabilities vary significantly by model and task. Claims about general intelligence remain dependent on definitions, evidence, and evaluation methods rather than on a single announcement.
8.1 Interpreting the timeline

The timeline should not be understood as a sequence in which each milestone completely replaced the previous one. Symbolic reasoning still matters. Statistical methods remain important. Deep learning builds on mathematics, computing, data, and earlier research. Modern systems often combine several techniques.

Three broad transitions are particularly important. First, early AI emphasized explicit symbols, rules, and search. Second, statistical machine learning increasingly enabled systems to learn patterns from examples. Third, deep learning and large-scale data and computing enabled major improvements in perception, speech, and language. These transitions overlap rather than form perfectly separate eras.

Another important lesson is that breakthroughs depend on infrastructure. Algorithms require data, computing, software tools, evaluation datasets, and engineering practices. A clever method may remain limited until the resources needed to use it become available.

sec.t: Categorization of AI: Narrow AI, General AI, and Super AI
sec.s: AI systems differ in the breadth of tasks they can perform.

b.x: 9.1 Why categorize AI?

AI systems differ in the breadth of tasks they can perform. Some are built for one narrow function; others can work across several related tasks; and some proposed categories describe hypothetical systems with capabilities exceeding human intelligence broadly. Categorizing systems helps distinguish current technology from future possibilities.

The common three-part classification is narrow AI, general AI, and super AI. This is primarily a classification by capability and scope, not a precise engineering standard. Definitions of general and super AI vary among researchers, and there is no universally accepted test that marks the exact boundary between them.
9.2 Narrow AI or Weak AI

Narrow AI refers to systems designed to perform a specific task or a limited group of tasks. “Weak” does not mean that the system is ineffective. A narrow system can outperform people in its chosen domain. The label indicates that its competence is limited in scope compared with general human intelligence.
Examples include

x: An email spam filter.
A recommendation system that suggests films or products.
A program that detects objects in photographs.
A speech-recognition system that converts audio into text.
A chess or Go engine.
A model that estimates credit risk.
A translation system.
A quality-control model that detects defects in manufactured goods.

b.x: Narrow AI is the dominant form of deployed AI. Even highly capable chatbots and multimodal assistants are generally classified as narrow AI under this broad taxonomy because their abilities depend on computational models, training processes, interfaces, and operating conditions. They can handle many tasks, but they are not established examples of human-level general intelligence across all domains.
Advantages of narrow AI

x: It can be optimized for a clearly defined goal.
It may achieve high accuracy and speed in its domain.
Its performance can often be measured using task-specific benchmarks.
It can automate repetitive work and support decisions.
It may be cheaper and easier to deploy than a broad general-purpose system.
It can be integrated into existing workflows.

b.x: Limitations of narrow AI

x: It may fail when input differs significantly from training data.
It may not transfer knowledge well to unrelated tasks.
It can depend on large amounts of labelled or representative data.
It may reproduce bias or errors in the data.
It may be difficult to interpret, depending on the method.
It needs monitoring when deployed in changing environments.

A model trained to detect pneumonia-related patterns in chest X-rays may help a clinical team prioritize cases. It is not automatically qualified to diagnose every disease, recommend all treatments, or replace a clinician. Its intended use, training data, validation, and limitations must be clearly specified.

b.x: 9.3 General AI or Strong AI

Artificial general intelligence (AGI), often associated with the term strong AI in popular discussion, refers to a hypothetical or not-yet-established level of AI capable of learning, reasoning, and performing a broad range of intellectual tasks with flexibility comparable to humans. The precise definition is debated. Some definitions emphasize human-level performance across many domains; others emphasize the ability to adapt to unfamiliar tasks and transfer knowledge.

A general system would need to do more than perform many tasks when separately trained for each one. It would ideally use knowledge acquired in one context to support learning in another, plan across extended activities, handle unfamiliar situations, and adapt when instructions or environments change.
Potential characteristics often discussed include

x: Broad problem-solving across domains.
Flexible learning and transfer of knowledge.
Reasoning under uncertainty.
Planning over long sequences of actions.
Learning new tasks with limited additional instruction.
Combining language, perception, and action.
Recognizing uncertainty and correcting mistakes.
Adapting to new environments.

b.x: These are research goals and proposed criteria, not a universally agreed checklist. A system can display some of these characteristics without satisfying all definitions of AGI.

Is AGI already achieved? There is no universally accepted answer because experts disagree about the definition, evaluation criteria, and significance of current capabilities. Modern models can perform a wide variety of tasks, but they also display failures in reliability, robustness, grounding, long-horizon planning, and other areas. It is therefore important to distinguish broad task coverage from dependable general intelligence.

Possible benefits of AGI, if developed safely, could include assistance with scientific research, education, engineering, medicine, accessibility, and complex planning. Potential risks could include misuse, economic disruption, loss of control over important processes, concentration of power, and errors at scale. These outcomes are not automatic; they depend on system design, access, governance, deployment, and human decisions.
9.4 Super AI or Artificial Superintelligence

Super AI, often called artificial superintelligence, describes a hypothetical system whose intellectual capabilities substantially exceed those of the best human minds across a broad range of domains. It is a speculative category rather than an established description of current systems.

In discussions of superintelligence, researchers sometimes consider capabilities such as scientific discovery, strategic planning, engineering, persuasion, learning, and problem-solving at levels far beyond human performance. The term can refer to a system that is much faster than people, much more capable across many domains, or able to improve its own capabilities. These possibilities are distinct and should not be assumed to occur together.

Potential benefits sometimes proposed include accelerating scientific discoveries, helping solve complex engineering problems, improving disease research, optimizing energy systems, and supporting responses to global challenges. Such benefits would depend on whether the system’s outputs were correct, its objectives were appropriately constrained, and institutions could use it safely.
Potential risks include

x: Misalignment between system objectives and human intentions.
Powerful capabilities being misused by people or organizations.
Unanticipated actions arising from complex system interactions.
Concentration of economic or political power.
Large-scale errors or failures.
Difficulties in monitoring and controlling systems that operate faster than human oversight can respond.

b.x: These are subjects of active debate. The existence, timeline, and characteristics of superintelligence are uncertain. It is inaccurate to describe super AI as an existing technology or to treat any one forecast as established fact.
9.5 Narrow AI versus AGI versus super AI

Narrow AI: designed for specific or limited tasks; it exists widely today. General AI: aims for broad, flexible competence across intellectual tasks; its status depends on disputed definitions and remains unconfirmed as a settled achievement. Super AI: hypothetical intelligence that exceeds human capabilities broadly; its existence and timeline are uncertain.

The difference is mainly breadth and adaptability, not merely speed. A calculator can be much faster than a human at arithmetic, but that does not make it generally intelligent. A chess engine can defeat any human player under some conditions, but it cannot thereby perform every other intellectual task. Superiority in one dimension is not the same as superiority across all dimensions.
9.6 Weak AI and strong AI: an important terminology warning

The terms “weak AI” and “strong AI” have sometimes been used in philosophy to distinguish a system that simulates intelligent behaviour from one that genuinely has a mind or understanding. In many introductory textbooks, however, weak AI is used as another name for narrow AI, while strong AI is used as another name for AGI. These usages overlap but are not perfectly identical.

When reading a source, check how it defines the terms. A debate about whether a machine truly understands language is different from a classification of whether it can perform many kinds of tasks. Clear definitions prevent confusion.

sec.t: Three Core Domains of AI: Data Science, Computer Vision, and Natural Language Processing
sec.s: An AI domain is an area of problems, data, methods, and applications.

b.x: 10.1 Understanding AI domains

An AI domain is an area of problems, data, methods, and applications. Data science, computer vision, and natural language processing are closely connected to AI, but they are not interchangeable terms.

Data science is a broad, interdisciplinary practice that uses data, statistics, computation, visualization, and domain knowledge to extract insights and support decisions. It may use AI and machine learning, but it also includes data collection, cleaning, descriptive analysis, experimentation, and reporting.

Computer vision is the field concerned with enabling computers to extract useful information from images and videos. It includes image classification, object detection, segmentation, tracking, and three-dimensional perception.

Natural language processing (NLP) focuses on computational processing of human language, including text and, in connected speech systems, language-related aspects of audio. Tasks include classification, translation, information extraction, summarization, question answering, and text generation.

These domains often work together. A retail company might use data science to analyze purchases, computer vision to inspect product images, and NLP to classify customer reviews. A medical system might analyze patient records with data-science methods, interpret radiology images with computer vision, and process clinical notes with NLP.

sec.s: Data science is the systematic process of collecting, preparing, exploring, analyzing, and interpreting…

b.x: 11.1 Definition and purpose

Data science is the systematic process of collecting, preparing, exploring, analyzing, and interpreting data to answer questions or support decisions. It combines statistics, programming, data management, visualization, machine learning, and knowledge of the problem domain.

Data science begins before model training. A successful project needs a clearly defined question, appropriate data, reliable measurements, careful cleaning, valid analysis, and an explanation of what the results mean. A sophisticated model cannot compensate for fundamentally incorrect or unrepresentative data.

For example, a university may want to understand why students miss classes. A data-science project could examine attendance, timetable patterns, course load, transport constraints, and survey responses. The aim would not simply be to produce a prediction; it would be to understand the problem and identify useful interventions.
11.2 Typical data-science workflow

x: Step 1

Define the problem. Specify the question and how success will be measured. “Improve student outcomes” is too broad by itself. A clearer question might be: “Can we identify students who may benefit from additional academic support early in the semester?” The goal should be useful, measurable, and ethically appropriate.
Step 2

Collect data. Data may come from databases, spreadsheets, sensors, surveys, public datasets, application logs, websites, or APIs. The source must be relevant and lawful to use. Collection should respect privacy, consent, access controls, and data-retention requirements.
Step 3

Understand the data. Inspect the number of records, columns, data types, ranges, missing values, duplicates, and possible errors. Metadata and documentation help explain how variables were collected. A column called “score” is not useful without knowing its scale, timing, and meaning.
Step 4

Clean and prepare the data. Preparation may involve correcting inconsistent formats, handling missing values, removing duplicates, resolving invalid records, encoding categories, normalizing numerical values, and checking for outliers. Cleaning decisions should be documented because they can affect the conclusions.
Step 5

Explore the data. Exploratory data analysis uses summaries and visualizations to identify distributions, relationships, unusual observations, and possible data-quality problems. It helps the analyst form hypotheses and detect mistakes before modelling.
Step 6

Build features. A feature is an input variable used by a model or analysis. Raw timestamps might be converted into day-of-week or time-of-day features. Text may be represented with numerical features or learned embeddings. Feature engineering should use information that would genuinely be available at prediction time.
Step 7

Split the data when modelling. A dataset is commonly divided into training, validation, and test sets. The training set is used to fit the model; validation data help compare approaches and tune settings; the test set provides a final evaluation on data not used for those decisions. The correct split depends on the task. Time-dependent data often require chronological splitting, while grouped data may require splitting by person, patient, or organization to avoid leakage.
Step 8

Train and compare models. Start with a simple baseline. More complex models should be used when they provide meaningful improvement. The choice depends on the target, data volume, interpretability needs, computation, and cost of errors.
Step 9

Evaluate. Choose metrics appropriate to the task. Classification may use precision, recall, F1 score, ROC-AUC, or other measures. Regression may use mean absolute error, mean squared error, or related metrics. No metric should be interpreted without considering class balance, error costs, and the real purpose of the model.
Step 10

Communicate findings. Results should be presented in a form that decision-makers can understand. Explain assumptions, uncertainty, limitations, and what action the evidence supports. Correlation does not automatically establish causation.
Step 11

Deploy and monitor when appropriate. A model used in production needs monitoring for performance changes, data drift, system failures, security problems, and unintended effects. Models may require retraining, recalibration, or withdrawal if conditions change.

b.x: 11.3 Types of data
Structured data are organized into defined rows and columns, such as a database table containing student IDs, course names, and marks. They are often easier to query and analyze with SQL.

Unstructured data do not fit neatly into conventional tables. Examples include images, audio, video, and free-form text. They often require specialized processing, although they can still be stored and managed using suitable systems.
Semi-structured data contain organizational markers but do not necessarily follow a rigid relational schema. JSON and XML are common examples.

Data can also be numerical or categorical. Numerical variables include age, temperature, and income. Categorical variables include course type, product category, or region. The choice of analysis depends on the data type and how the variable was measured.
11.4 The role of statistics

Statistics provides tools for summarizing data, estimating uncertainty, testing hypotheses, and understanding relationships. A mean describes a form of central tendency, while variance and standard deviation describe dispersion. Sampling methods influence whether findings can be generalized to a wider population.

Statistical reasoning also helps prevent overinterpretation. A difference in average scores may arise from chance, confounding variables, measurement problems, or selection effects. A model’s prediction is not automatically a causal explanation.
11.5 Machine learning within data science

Machine learning is useful when patterns in data can support prediction, classification, clustering, ranking, or decision-making. In supervised classification, a model learns from examples with known labels. In regression, it predicts a numerical value. In clustering, it groups examples based on similarities without relying on the same kind of predefined labels. In anomaly detection, it identifies observations that differ from expected patterns.

A student learning AI should distinguish data preparation from model creation. Loading a dataset is not the same as training a model. A reliable pipeline may include reading the data, checking its structure, cleaning records, encoding labels, splitting the data, transforming inputs, training a model, evaluating results, and saving the fitted components for later use.
11.6 Common data-science problems
Data leakage occurs when information unavailable at real prediction time accidentally enters training or evaluation. This can make performance look much better than it will be in deployment.

Class imbalance occurs when one category is much more common than another. A model can achieve high accuracy by predicting the majority class while failing to identify rare but important cases. Precision, recall, class-specific metrics, appropriate sampling, and suitable loss functions may help.

Sampling bias occurs when the collected data do not represent the population to which conclusions will be applied. Missing-data problems can also distort analysis if the absence of a value is related to the underlying phenomenon.

Overfitting occurs when a model learns details specific to the training data rather than patterns that generalize. Underfitting occurs when a model is too simple or poorly trained to capture important relationships. Separate evaluation data and sensible model selection help identify these problems.
11.7 Applications of data science

Data science supports demand forecasting, fraud detection, logistics, marketing analysis, energy management, medical research, scientific modelling, public-service planning, and recommendation systems. It can reveal patterns that would be difficult to identify manually.

Its limitations are equally important. Data can be inaccurate, biased, incomplete, outdated, or collected for a different purpose. A prediction can affect people unfairly if used without proper context. Human review, privacy protections, clear documentation, and ongoing evaluation are essential in sensitive applications.

sec.s: Computer vision is a field of computing and AI that develops methods for extracting information from…

b.x: 12.1 Definition

Computer vision is a field of computing and AI that develops methods for extracting information from images and videos. The goal may be to identify what is present, locate objects, measure shapes, understand motion, reconstruct a scene, or support a decision.

A digital image can be represented as a grid of pixels. Each pixel stores numerical values that represent intensity or colour. A computer-vision model processes these values and attempts to infer useful information. Modern methods often learn visual representations from examples, while traditional approaches may use explicitly designed features and image-processing operations.
12.2 Main computer-vision tasks

A. Image classification Classification assigns a label to an entire image or crop. For example, a model may classify an image as containing a cat, dog, car, or tree. The output may be a class label or scores associated with several classes.

B. Object detection Object detection identifies objects and estimates their locations, commonly using bounding boxes. A road-scene model might detect cars, cyclists, pedestrians, and traffic signs. Detection is more informative than image classification because it indicates where objects appear.

C. Image segmentation Segmentation assigns labels to pixels or regions. Semantic segmentation labels each pixel by category, such as road, building, or vegetation. Instance segmentation additionally distinguishes separate objects belonging to the same category. Segmentation is useful when precise boundaries matter.

D. Object tracking Tracking follows objects across successive video frames. A system may maintain an identity for a moving vehicle or person as the scene changes. Tracking combines detection with temporal information and may need to handle occlusion, motion blur, and changing appearance.

E. Optical character recognition OCR converts text in images into machine-readable characters. It is used for scanned documents, receipts, forms, signs, and printed pages. Accuracy can be affected by low resolution, unusual fonts, handwriting, skew, and poor lighting.

F. Pose estimation Pose estimation identifies key points or body positions, such as the location of joints in a human figure. It can support sports analysis, motion studies, animation, and some human-computer interaction applications.

G. Three-dimensional vision Three-dimensional vision estimates depth, shape, or spatial relationships. Methods may use stereo cameras, depth sensors, motion, or learned representations. It is important in robotics, mapping, industrial inspection, and autonomous navigation.
12.3 How a computer-vision system works

A typical learning-based vision pipeline begins with data collection. Images must represent the intended environment and be labelled when the training method requires labels. Labels might identify the image class, draw bounding boxes, or mark pixels belonging to different objects.

Images are then preprocessed. Common operations include resizing, normalization, and data augmentation. Augmentation creates altered training examples, such as flipped, cropped, or slightly rotated images, when those changes preserve the correct label and match plausible conditions.

A model is trained on the prepared data. Convolutional neural networks have been widely used because convolutional operations can learn spatial patterns. Vision Transformers and other architectures also play important roles. During training, the model’s parameters are updated to reduce a loss function that measures the difference between predictions and target labels.

The model is evaluated on data kept separate from training. Evaluation should reflect realistic conditions, not merely a random collection of nearly identical images. Finally, the model may be integrated into an application and monitored after deployment.
12.4 Why deep learning transformed computer vision

Traditional vision methods often relied on hand-designed features and task-specific processing. Deep learning allowed systems to learn useful features directly from large collections of images. Early layers in a network may learn simple patterns, while later layers can represent more complex structures. This hierarchy is not a perfect explanation of every model, but it offers an intuitive picture of representation learning.

The 2012 AlexNet result on ImageNet was a major milestone because it demonstrated the practical value of deep convolutional networks at scale. Progress depended not only on the network design but also on labelled data, GPU computing, training methods, and evaluation infrastructure.
12.5 Applications of computer vision

x: Healthcare
Vision systems can assist with analyzing radiology, pathology, and other medical images. They must be validated carefully because false positives and false negatives can have serious consequences.
Manufacturing
Cameras and models can inspect products for scratches, cracks, missing parts, or assembly defects. Controlled lighting and consistent camera positions can improve reliability.
Agriculture

Vision can help identify plant disease symptoms, estimate crop conditions, monitor weeds, or guide agricultural robots. Field conditions introduce variation in weather, lighting, and plant appearance.
Transportation
Vision systems can detect road users, lanes, signs, and obstacles. Safety-critical systems require extensive testing and cannot rely on a single model in isolation.
Retail and logistics
Vision can support inventory counting, package sorting, barcode reading, and automated inspection.
Accessibility
Image-description systems and OCR can help users access visual information, though descriptions can be incomplete or incorrect and should be treated accordingly.
Security and public spaces
Face and object recognition technologies can support specific security tasks but raise serious concerns about privacy, surveillance, consent, demographic performance differences, and misuse.

b.x: 12.6 Challenges in computer vision

Lighting changes can alter an image dramatically. Shadows, glare, weather, blur, camera angle, and occlusion can reduce performance. A model trained on one environment may not generalize to another. This is an example of distribution shift.

A dataset may also contain hidden shortcuts. For example, a model might associate a background with a category instead of learning the object itself. It may perform well on test images drawn from the same source but fail in a different setting.

Labels can be expensive and inconsistent. Two annotators may disagree about the boundary of an object or the correct category. Privacy is another concern when images contain faces, homes, license plates, or sensitive locations.
Computer vision should therefore be evaluated using diverse and representative data, clear definitions of success, careful privacy practices, and monitoring in the target environment.

sec.s: Natural language processing (NLP) is the area of computing concerned with enabling computers to process,…

b.x: 13.1 Definition

Natural language processing (NLP) is the area of computing concerned with enabling computers to process, analyze, interpret, and generate human language. Human language is difficult for machines because words can be ambiguous, meanings depend on context, grammar varies, and people use sarcasm, idioms, incomplete sentences, and cultural references.

NLP includes both language understanding tasks and language generation tasks. Systems may classify a message, extract information, translate a sentence, summarize a document, answer a question, or generate a response. NLP can work with written text and can connect to speech technologies that convert audio to text or text to speech.
13.2 Text representation

Computers process numerical representations, so text must be converted into forms that algorithms can use. Early NLP often relied on counts of words, hand-built rules, and linguistic features. Modern systems frequently use tokenization and learned vector representations.

Tokenization divides text into units called tokens. A token may be a word, part of a word, punctuation, or another unit depending on the tokenizer. For example, an uncommon word may be split into multiple subword tokens. Tokenization is not the same as assigning meaning; it is a preprocessing step that determines how text is represented for the model.

A vocabulary maps tokens to numerical IDs. Padding may be used to make sequences in a batch the same length. Attention masks commonly indicate which positions are actual tokens and which are padding, though the precise convention depends on the model and library. These details matter when building and training language models.
13.3 Common NLP tasks

A. Text classification Text classification assigns a category to a text. Examples include spam detection, sentiment analysis, topic classification, and routing a customer-support request to the correct department.

B. Sentiment analysis Sentiment analysis estimates the expressed attitude or emotional polarity in text, often using categories such as positive, negative, or neutral. Real sentiment is more complex: sarcasm, mixed opinions, cultural context, and indirect language can make classification difficult.

C. Named-entity recognition Named-entity recognition identifies spans of text that refer to categories such as people, organizations, locations, dates, or monetary values. It can help extract structured information from news, reports, and documents.

D. Machine translation Machine translation converts text from one language to another. Modern systems often use neural networks and Transformer architectures. Translation quality depends on language pair, domain, context, training data, and the need to preserve tone or technical meaning.

E. Summarization Summarization creates a shorter representation of a longer text. Extractive methods select portions of the original, while abstractive methods generate new wording. Summaries must preserve important meaning and avoid inventing details.

F. Question answering Question-answering systems respond to questions using a passage, database, model knowledge, or external tools. Reliability depends on the source of information, retrieval quality, and whether the system can distinguish evidence from uncertainty.

G. Information extraction Information extraction converts unstructured text into structured fields or relationships. For example, a system might extract a company name, date, product, and reported price from an article.

H. Text generation Text-generation systems produce new text based on an input prompt or conversation context. They can assist with drafting, explanation, coding, brainstorming, and summarization. Generated output may nevertheless contain factual errors, unsupported claims, or unsuitable content.
13.4 From rules to statistical NLP
